title: Health Checks
description: Learn how load balancers detect unhealthy servers, configure active and passive health checks, and avoid false positives in production systems.

data.text: Health checks allow a load balancer to determine whether a backend server is healthy and capable of serving traffic. Without reliable health checks, users may receive errors even when other servers are functioning normally. A good health check strategy balances detection speed with false-positive risk.

Active health checks are initiated by the load balancer itself. The balancer periodically sends a request to a dedicated endpoint, such as /healthz or /status, and marks the server unhealthy if the response is incorrect or too slow. This is the most common mechanism in cloud and Kubernetes environments.

data.title: Best Practice
data.text: Health check endpoints should be lightweight and independent from main application logic. Avoid expensive database calls inside /healthz.

Passive health checks observe real traffic. If a server repeatedly returns 5xx errors or drops connections, the load balancer removes it from rotation without any probe overhead. Passive checks are useful for detecting application-level failures that active probes may miss.

data.caption: Active and passive health check flow in a load-balanced environment.
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    participant LB as Load Balancer
    participant S1 as Server 1
    participant S2 as Server 2
    LB->>S1: Periodic /healthz probe
    alt Healthy response
        S1-->>LB: 200 OK
        LB->>S1: Continue routing traffic
    else Unhealthy response
        S1-->>LB: 500 / timeout
        LB->>S1: Mark unhealthy
    end
    LB->>S2: Monitor live requests
    alt 5xx observed
        S2-->>LB: 5xx error
        LB->>S2: Remove from rotation

data.title: Health check configuration
items: Set intervals based on acceptable failover time.
Use multiple failed checks before marking unhealthy to reduce false positives.
Require several consecutive successes before returning a server to rotation.

terms.definition: A dedicated HTTP or TCP endpoint used to report service health.
The number of consecutive failures required to mark a backend as unhealthy.
A failure detected through observed traffic rather than active probing.

data.title: Takeaway
points: Active probes catch failures early but add overhead.
Passive checks detect real-world failures with no extra traffic.
Threshold tuning reduces false positives and flapping.
data.takeaway: Effective health checks combine active probes with passive observation and careful threshold tuning.
